issues.item: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile as a coherent pattern for a trauma-to-a-loved-one case: 'Cars hit by accident' suggests a specific road-traffic trauma cue, while 'Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place' implies separation/safety-context triggering. These could coexist, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content about separation, they look clinically mismatched within the trigger node.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory items describe vivid sensory re-experiencing of a frightening event, and the other appraisals emphasize unfairness and generalized vigilance, but nothing else suggests interpersonal betrayal. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one formulation, this appraisal would usually require supporting context (e.g. trusted person caused or enabled the harm), which is absent here.

The trigger profile is only weakly coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Workplace' as a major trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved-one trauma happened in the workplace or through occupational exposure, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other triggers (cars hit by accident, alcohol smell) imply a specific accident scene, making 'workplace' stand out as clinically questionable rather than part of the same trigger network.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Betrayal by someone I trusted' points toward an interpersonal trauma formulation, but the rest of the profile centers on sensory accident-related reminders and vivid perceptual memory. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this appraisal is difficult to integrate unless the loved one's trauma directly involved trusted-person betrayal, which is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node contains two items that are hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with each other. 'Constant Vigilance' implies an ongoing sense of current danger, but the formulation has no active Threat links and the rest of the profile is focused on accident-related reminders and vivid sensory memory rather than present threat. 'Self-Blame' is also difficult to fit with a loved-one accident trauma in this profile, because no other item suggests the patient had a causally responsible role in the event; combined with the injustice item, it creates a mixed appraisal pattern that lacks a clear coherent basis in the rest of the report.

issues.item: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, strong endorsement of both injustice/external blame ('nothing has been done about it') and self-blame for causing the event pulls in opposing directions and is difficult to reconcile as the same dominant appraisal without additional context. For a trauma to a loved one, these two appraisals can coexist in milder form, but selected together as core items they suggest conflicting attribution styles within the same node.

vignette:
For forty-two years, Leilani had worn her police uniform as a second skin, a symbol of her role as a protector in her community. At seventy-one, she was the veteran everyone looked up to, steady and unflappable. That persona shattered six months ago, on a warm Saturday evening at a family barbeque in her own backyard. Her grandson, celebrating a new job, had had too much to drink. Leilani smelled the beer on his breath when he came to hug her goodbye and told him not to drive. They argued, his youthful pride clashing with her authority, and he had stormed off to his car. She was still standing on the porch, frozen between her roles as grandmother and officer, when she heard the screech of tires and the sickening, final sound of impact just two blocks away.

The memory of that night never comes to her as a linear story. Instead, it lives in her as a collection of sensory fragments. Her memories are overwhelmingly visual—brutal, high-definition snapshots of the crumpled driver-side door, the shattered glass glittering on the asphalt under the streetlights. These images are so clear and detailed that she can recall the specific pattern of the crack in the windshield. Sometimes, when the house is quiet, the memory is auditory; she hears the percussive crunch of metal, a sound that seems to vibrate deep in her chest, followed by her own raw scream. Because these fragments are so vivid and intrusive, her mind has learned to treat the world as a minefield of potential reminders. The sight or sound of anything that echoes that night has become an immediate and potent trigger for her distress.

This hypervigilance has made her job, once a source of pride, a source of constant torment. Responding to a routine traffic accident is now unbearable. The sight of any car hit in an accident, even a minor fender-bender, doesn't just remind her of the event; it activates a cascade of crushing self-blame. As she looks at the damaged vehicles, the thought is immediate and absolute: *The event happened because of the way I acted. I should have physically stopped him.* This conviction that she failed in her duty to protect her own family has become a central belief. The smell of alcohol, once just a common scent in her line of work, is now a direct indictment. Catching a whiff from a driver at a traffic stop sends a jolt through her, instantly reinforcing the appraisal that she is fundamentally helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to the people she loves most.

Over the past few months, these connections have forged a debilitating cycle. She started finding reasons to stay at the desk, avoiding patrol calls that might involve a collision. When her colleagues talk about accidents, particularly DUIs, she has to physically leave the room. The conversation itself acts as a trigger, bringing forth the images and sounds, which in turn feed her certainty that she is to blame. She had come to believe that she not only failed her grandson but that she is a fraud as an officer, a protector who cannot protect. Her marriage has grown strained under the weight of her silence and withdrawal. She feels she can no longer be the strong matriarch of her family, convinced she has forfeited that right.

Leilani has sought therapy because she received a formal warning about her performance at work, and she knows she cannot continue this way. She is terrified of being forced into retirement, not because she wants to keep working, but because leaving the force would feel like a final admission of her failure. More than anything, she is desperate for a way to quiet the images and sounds in her head, to stop the relentless loop of self-blame that begins the moment she encounters any reminder of the night she believes she lost not only her grandson, but herself.
